doc.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Playing for himself, honesty and what sells
summary: He plays for himself to grow, calls pop junk, Oprah example, and praises Jerry Bergonzi and Diz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well check this out, Monk, if I play — do you know something, like, take something that you really hate, you can’t stand musically, and you have to do something, and you put it on and it plays over and over again. You know what your mind will do? Your mind, especially you being a musician, your mind will find something in that thing to like, to grow with. Okay? And what’s happening, like my saying that I say — blessed are those that run around in circles, for they shall be called big wheels — these people at the radio stations, they don’t know their butts from holes in the ground. And those are the people that are choosing the music to play for people. If I give you something that I think you’ll want, I haven’t given you anything. But if I give you something that I know is good, and I feel that it can help you grow spiritually or something, and I give you that, I’ve given you something. When I play for a person, I don’t play for you. I play for me. And the reason I play for me is because I want to play better today, and I want to play better tomorrow than I did today. By that I’m saying I want to grow, musically and spiritually. So when I’m playing for you, I’m giving you honesty. But if I see you and I figure you want to hear me moan and whoa — and scream, because that’ll get you, I’m being dishonest. And for me, that isn’t music see? Music consists of three things: melody, harmony and rhythm. One thing alone doesn’t make music okay? So all that other stuff that they play on the radio for people, because they think it makes big bucks, yeah, but you know what? It makes big bucks but you watch, it’s also tearing down the moral fiber of youthfulness. I mean in other words the young kids are being like smothered with — excuse me, the only way I could — with bullshit. And you know that saying, if you can’t dazzle them with brilliance, baffle them with bullshit. You’ve heard that saying. Well that’s what’s happening today. Not only musically, but every which way.

In medicine, in every which way. Because first of all, look at Oprah. Any time a person can’t say well oh yeah, wow, well I’ll be damned. Beef is that bad? Well you know what? I think I’ll never eat another hamburger again. That’s because she has a show and somebody — because look, twenty million people calling a television set an automobile doesn’t make it one. But, if something is good for you, and you like it, I don’t care what somebody says about it, I’m going to still do it, see? So like if beef is all that good for you, people are going to eat it, but because Oprah said she didn’t want to eat a hamburger, they’re suing her for ten million dollars. In Texas you see. And if you notice, anything that’s really good, if you notice the good stuff is not there. Musically or any other way. You ever notice that? I mean the guys that could really play — I always say the greatest are yet to be heard. You know because the guys that play their buns off man, you don’t hear them that much. Look at Jerry Bergonzi.

Jerry Bergonzi. Oh man, isn’t he bad? But hear him man, boy I mean he’s playing some stuff, you know what I mean? I look at — oh thank you very much — look at Diz. Like people want to forget about him like he never existed. But —
